sections.heading: Abstract
sections.where: Title page, White Paper v1.2, July 29, 2026
paragraphs: The paper introduces Alpenglow as a consensus protocol for a worldwide proof-of-stake blockchain, aimed at high throughput and short finality. Votor, the voting component, is claimed to finalize a block in one round when "80%" of the stake participates, and in two rounds when only "60%" of the stake responds. The two modes run concurrently. Once a block has been distributed, the paper writes the resulting time as "min(δ80%, 2δ60%)".

Block distribution is Rotor, an erasure-coded broadcast that spends the outgoing bandwidth of participating nodes in proportion to their stake, so the leader is not the only sender of payload. The paper claims the total available bandwidth is used asymptotically optimally. Resilience is named "20+20": the protocol is said to tolerate harsh network conditions and an adversary with "20%" of the stake, and another "20%" of the stake may be offline when the network assumptions are stronger.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
paragraphs: The introduction rearranges a disputed remark often linked to an IBM president and treats the result as a market for a few world computers. A world computer, as defined here, takes transactions and updates a shared book for users everywhere, while the computer itself is spread across the internet. The paper puts that spread at hundreds or thousands of processors. It claims two advantages over one powerful machine: many component crashes can be survived, and no authority, including a hostile botnet, should be able to corrupt the machine for other users. The name it gives this machine is a blockchain.

Alpenglow is the protocol proposed for that machine. Rotor is described as an optimized and simplified descendant of Solana's Turbine, which the paper credits with bringing erasure-coded information dispersal to permissionless blockchains. Because Rotor uses the bandwidth the nodes provide, throughput is called asymptotically optimal. Protocols that leave a leader bandwidth bottleneck are said to suffer low throughput. Votor is said to take the simple structure of the Simplex line into proof of stake, so leaders rotate without a complicated view change. In the common case the paper claims one voting round, with a two-round procedure running at the same time as backup.

sections.heading: 1.1 Alpenglow Overview
paragraphs: The overview fixes the participants and the schedule before the algorithms. Alpenglow runs on n nodes, possibly thousands, known and fixed for an interval called an "epoch". Any node can send a direct message to any other. Each node has a known stake. The paper says a node with twice another node's stake earns twice the fees and provides twice the outgoing bandwidth. Time is partitioned into numbered slots. Each slot has a leader drawn from the nodes, and each leader is in charge for a fixed run of consecutive slots, a "leader window; a threshold VRF selects the schedule.

During its window the leader receives new transactions from users or from other nodes and builds a block. A block is cut into slices so production can overlap transmission, and each slice is cut into shreds so loss can be tolerated and the send load can be spread. Rotor, which erasure-codes those shreds, is what the leader uses to fan them out. Relays receive the shreds and pass them on. The stated aim is stake-proportional outgoing capacity, with no single leader pipe. The following leader may begin its own block the moment the current one is finished. Shreds and slices of incoming blocks are stored in "Blokstor".

Nodes vote on whether they support a block. Several vote types and aggregated certificates are defined later and stored in a local structure called "Pool". A timely, well-formed block receives a supporting vote. A late block receives a skip vote, which the overview treats as a sign that the leader is unreliable or the network is unstable. A large enough share of stake can lock the block in at once. Otherwise a further voting round decides whether to skip. The overview then points to leader logic for choosing a parent, to Repair for missing shreds, slices, or ancestor blocks, and to rejoining after a node loses contact.

The same overview maps the rest of the paper. Correctness is safety under an unreliable network, liveness under a reliable network, and a high number of crashes. Severe failures ask what happens if faults exceed "20%" or "40%", for the network and for software. The body of the design is said not to be secure against a quantum adversary, and a later section outlines the modifications, then their effect on Rotor and Votor. A final section is described as important for understanding and not required for correctness: relay sampling, how transactions are executed, parameter choices, and simulations of bandwidth and latency using Solana's node and stake distribution. Preliminaries close the introduction: fault-tolerance goals, performance metrics, related work, the model, and cryptography.

sections.heading: 1.2 Fault Tolerance
paragraphs: Safety is called the first objective. The usual target recalled here is resilience against adversaries controlling up to "33%" of the stake, the bound the paper calls "3f+1". That bound comes from work on small systems and still holds for large n, but the authors argue that attacking thousands of nodes is a different undertaking from attacking one or two. Running a thousand byzantine nodes would they say, likely require billions of dollars of staking capital, and misbehavior is often punishable, so the attacker would lose that capital. At this scale they expect the faults that actually show up to come from bad configuration, buggy software, and lost connectivity or power, and they treat those as accidents far more often than as a planned campaign.

That shift is the stated reason to use a "5f+1" bound from earlier fast-consensus papers. The paper says the bound is less tolerant of orthodox byzantine attacks. Two voting rounds become necessary to finalize when the adversary is powerful. If the adversary holds smaller stake, or fails to misbehave continuously, a correct protocol of this kind can finalize in a single round. Assumption 1 is the hypothesis used for the main correctness sections: Byzantine actors hold under 20% of stake, and the remaining nodes, controlling more than "80%", are correct.

Alpenglow is partially synchronous. Under Assumption 1 the paper claims that an adversary who completely controls the network, inspecting, delaying, and scheduling communication among correct nodes, still cannot violate safety. An outage or partition is said to pause the protocol and let it continue once communication returns, without an incorrect outcome. If the network is not attacked that way, Assumption 2 allows more crashes: byzantine stake remains under "20%", other nodes with up to "20%" of stake might crash, and the remaining nodes, more than "60%" of stake, are correct. The difference between the two assumptions is explained in the crash section.

sections.heading: 1.3 Performance Metrics
paragraphs: The latency claim is that after a block is distributed, finalization takes "min(δ80%, 2δ60%)". The symbol δθ is a network delay among a stake-weighted fraction θ of the nodes. An "80%" mechanism and a "60%" mechanism run concurrently. A low-latency cluster holding "60%" is described as likely to finish the two-delay path first, while more remote nodes may finish on the single-delay path, which is why the paper takes the minimum. Low latency is tied to usability: faster transaction finality and results for users with less delay.

Throughput is measured in transaction bytes per second or in transactions per second. The paper says the protocol uses total available bandwidth asymptotically optimally. After those two metrics, it also wants protocol overhead minimized, including computation and other resources. Simplicity is a further goal. The paper says simplicity is hard to quantify and still desirable, because it makes correctness, implementation, upgrades, and optimization easier.

sections.heading: 1.4 Related Work
paragraphs: Related protocols are described as originally published. On bandwidth, PBFT, Tendermint, and HotStuff are cited as designs in which one leader disseminates the payload to all replicas, a bottleneck the paper calls a defining limit on throughput. DAG protocols have all nodes disseminate data, and the paper says they exhibit a latency penalty. Some reduce that penalty by forgoing certification of the disseminated data. Mysticeti is described as confirming a leader block in two voting rounds, after dissemination and two referencing layers, counted here as "3δ". Most data, meaning non-leader blocks, is ordered when a leader block certifying it is finalized, counted as "5δ". The paper notes published concerns that this technique affects robustness.

Erasure coding is presented as another way to relieve the leader bottleneck. The leader encodes the payload into fragments, different nodes help disseminate them, and bandwidth use is meant to be balanced. Solana is credited with pioneering this in blockchains, and Alpenglow follows that line. A cited comparison framework is said to indicate that payload erasure coding, as in DispersedSimplex,, beats DAG designs on latency. A second contributor to throughput is parallel execution. Distributed schemes such as Pilotfish and Stingray divide execution across machines and can scale horizontally when the workload parallelizes well. The paper says that potential is typically very limited on DeFi workloads, so one machine can saturate it.

Parallel execution is split into read-write oblivious, called optimistic, and read-write aware, called pessimistic. Optimistic execution, with Block-STM as the example, runs transactions in parallel and re-executes on conflicts. The paper says repeated rollbacks damage this style when many transactions conflict, and it names DeFi as that kind of load. Solana is credited with pioneering pessimistic parallel execution in blockchains, using user-provided read and write sets to derive conflicts so each transaction executes once.

On latency, the paper reviews protocols that finish after one voting round, often called fast or one-step consensus. DGV and FaB Paxos introduce "3f+2p+1" replicas, where p counts replicas the fast path does not need. They are said to terminate in "2δ", two network delays, under optimistic conditions. Later work is described as pointing out liveness and safety issues in landmark papers. SBFT is said to have addressed those correctness issues: it can finish after one voting round, and it is optimized for linear message complexity, which incurs higher latency. The paper says the "3f+2p+1" lower bound applies only to a restricted protocol type, and that some single-shot protocols use "3f+2p*−1" replicas, with the star parameter at least 1.

In practice, the paper says a one-round vote among the wider replica set can be slower than two rounds among a geographically tighter set. Banyan is described as renewing interest in fast Byzantine fault tolerance by running a one-round mechanism and a two-round mechanism in parallel, so the best latency is obtained. Kudzu is presented as the research companion of Alpenglow. It uses a thinner model, appeared just after version 1.0, and likewise combines coded dissemination with a one-round path running beside a two-round path.

The listed differences are as follows. Kudzu is permissioned and Alpenglow is proof of stake, and the paper says erasure-coded dissemination does not translate between those models merely by changing voting weights. Alpenglow uses leader windows in which the leader streams data without interruption, and concurrent processing lets block times be shorter than the latency bound ∆. On rotation, the next leader can start once the prior block has arrived. Under Assumption 3, Alpenglow is said to have higher resilience to crash faults. Kudzu nodes may vote on the first fragment of a proposal, while Alpenglow participants ballot only after rebuilding a complete proposal. The paper calls the former faster in theory and the practical difference a fraction of one network delay. Alpenglow can set the erasure-coding expansion freely and suggests a ratio of 2, while Kudzu requires a higher ratio.

Hydrangea is later work that parametrizes byzantine and crash faults in a related way. It requires a node count of 3f plus 2c plus k plus 1, and while the network is only partially synchronous, it withstands f byzantine faults together with c crashes. The count of nodes that one-round finalization may skip is derived from c and k. The floor expression is typographically flattened in the extract, while the example is explicit. To terminate in one round among "80%" of nodes, the paper says Hydrangea would set that skipped count, c, and k each to "20%" and f to "13%", for "33%" faulty nodes in total. Alpenglow is said to tolerate f under "20%" and "40%" faulty nodes in total, and to need Assumption 3 for fault rates above "20%". The paper says Hydrangea still has a leader bandwidth bottleneck and remains underspecified for practical implementation, while the parametrization could also be applied to Alpenglow.

sections.heading: 1.5 Model and Preliminaries
paragraphs: A named object with parameters means a deterministic encoding of that type and those parameters. Epochs let the participant set change. They are numbered starting at 1. The nodes and their stake for epoch e plus 1 get locked when epoch e minus 1, so agreement on the set is already in place when the new epoch begins. The machines are nodes, sometimes called validators because they relay messages and validate blocks. The set is fixed during an epoch and public: every node knows every address, port, and public key. That record is announced and updated by a transaction on the chain. The paper says Solana has about "1,500" nodes, that the protocol can in principle scale higher, and that a cap at some nmax may be useful in practice.

Nodes exchange authenticated messages. The document states that every message stays under "1,500" bytes. Transport is therefore UDP with authentication, either QUIC-UDP or UDP plus a pairwise message authentication code. Symmetric keys come from a key exchange on the public keys. A broadcast is simply a loop over the other nodes, and the document notes that network delay still dominates that loop. Voting traffic is described as shorter once delays sit near "2" milliseconds. A stake-weighted latency figure δ_θ is defined for a stake threshold θ, and that quantity appears again in the performance claims. Those timing and size figures are the document’s model assumptions, not measurements taken for this reading.

Each node has a positive stake fraction, fixed during the epoch, and the fractions sum to 1. Twice the stake means roughly twice the fees and twice the outgoing bandwidth. Every node still needs enough incoming bandwidth to receive blocks, and some minimum outgoing bandwidth for the slots it leads. Each node has a local clock. The paper gives "50 ppm" as an example of reasonable accuracy, leaves drift out of the analysis, and says drift can be absorbed into timeouts. Clocks need not be synchronized, because a node measures only its own short intervals.

A slot is a natural number associated with a block. It does not require nodes to agree on timing, so the same slot can start at different local times, though the paper expects rough alignment in normal conditions. An epoch runs through slots 1 to L. Solana's parameter L equal to "432,000" is called possible, and a much shorter epoch, for example "18,000" slots, is called advantageous when stake should change more quickly. The leader of each slot is a deterministic function known before the epoch. That leader's consecutive slots are the leader window. A threshold VRF, evaluated before the epoch, produces the public schedule.

Timeouts keep the protocol from waiting forever. They are based on a global ∆, the maximum delay between any two correct nodes while the network is synchronous. Durations may change with conditions, and the paper says the protocol stays correct regardless of the ∆ the network exhibits. The analysis treats ∆ as a constant, with "200 ms" as the example. Timeouts measure short local periods, so wall-clock time and skew are said to have no significance. Extreme drift is incorporated into the timeout. The example is that "5%" drift is handled by extending timeouts "5%". Because the protocol is partially synchronous, the paper says timing and clock errors cannot derail it.

Byzantine nodes may behave arbitrarily. They may fail to send a message, and they may collude. Some misbehavior, such as signing conflicting data can constitute a provable offense. Other misbehavior, such as sending late, may be impossible to punish, because an extraordinary delay can be innocent. All Byzantine actors collectively hold strictly under 20% of stake under Assumption 1. Up to an additional "20%" may crash under the later crash conditions. The analysis of safety, liveness, and crashes treats the adversary as static over one epoch. The network is the partial-synchrony model with an unknown global stabilization time. Messages between correct nodes eventually arrive and may take arbitrarily long before that time. Safety is always claimed: arbitrary delay still leaves every correct node emitting one common sequence of blocks.

Liveness is claimed only when the network is synchronous and messages arrive in time, meaning correct nodes keep outputting transactions in those periods. After the unknown stabilization time, a message sent at a given time arrives by the later of that stabilization time and the send time, plus ∆. During synchrony the paper expects the protocol rarely to wait out a timeout. Actual delay is written δ, much smaller than ∆, variable, and unknown. It is used for latency discussion only. Common-case performance is said to depend on δ and not on ∆. The delay δθ is the time in which every node of some set with stake at least θ sends a message to every other node of that set. If "60%" of stake is geographically close, the paper says two such delays can be less time than one delay that involves "80%" of stake.

The purpose stated for the blockchain is a sequence of finalized blocks of transactions, with all nodes outputting transactions in the same order. Every block has a parent, starting from a notional genesis block, and finalized blocks form one chain of parent links. Finalizing a block finalizes its ancestors. The slot of a child is numerically above the slot of its parent. Every slot contributes either a leader block that can become final or an explicit skip. Finalized blocks reach the execution layer in slot order. The safety guarantee is that if a correct node finalizes block b in slot s, then any block finalized by a correct node in a slot at least s is a descendant of b. The liveness guarantee is that in any long enough period of synchrony, correct honest participants finalize fresh blocks that honest leaders produced. Those statements are the two later theorems.

sections.heading: 1.6 Cryptographic Techniques
paragraphs: The toolkit begins with a collision-resistant hash, SHA-256 given as the example, and with unforgeable digital signatures. Every node knows every other node's public key. Signatures from different signers on the same message may be combined without interaction into an aggregate. BLS is named as one implementation. The paper says aggregates let certificates fit in a short message while the node count stays at most nmax. An erasure code with parameters Γ at least γ at least 1 encodes a string of length m as Γ pieces of length m over γ, plus an indexing overhead of order log Γ. Any γ pieces reconstruct the string. The length is treated as constant by padding shorter payloads. A slice uses a Reed-Solomon code of this form, and the expansion rate κ is Γ divided by γ.

A Merkle tree commits to the vector of pieces. Each leaf is the hash of a piece concatenated with a label that marks it as a leaf, and each internal node equals H(left_child || right_child); that top hash is the commitment. The validation path for a position is the sequence of sibling hashes from that leaf up to the root. Recomputing the path and matching the given root shows that the piece occupies that position. Collision resistance is what rules out a different piece with a valid proof for the same position.

The encode function erasure-codes the payload, builds the tree, and returns the root with every piece and path. The decode function takes the root and γ pieces whose paths check. It reconstructs a candidate, encodes that candidate again, and accepts it only if the recomputed root matches. On failure, the paper says no γ pieces tied to that root will decode, and the root was maliciously constructed.

sections.heading: 2 The Alpenglow Protocol
paragraphs: Section 2 is the detailed protocol. Its opening figure places Blokstor next to Repair, Pool next to block creation, and Votor next to Rotor and broadcast. The arrows are three flows: block data as shreds, internal events, and votes or certificates. The subsections then define shreds, slices, and blocks, the dissemination procedure, the two local stores, the voting loop, how a leader builds blocks, how missing data is repaired, and how a node joins.

sections.heading: 2.1 Shred, Slice, Block
paragraphs: A shred is defined to fit in one UDP datagram. Its fields are the slot number, the slice index, the shred index, a flag bit, the slice Merkle root, the data at that shred index with its Merkle path, and the signature of the slot's leader. The signed object names the slice by slot, index, flag, and root. A slice is the input of one Rotor transmission. Any γ of its Γ shreds decode the slice. The flag indicates the last slice of the slot. The decoded payload and the same leader signature are part of the slice.

A block is the sequence of all slices of one slot, and it is what nodes vote on. The last slice has the flag set, and every earlier slice has the flag clear. Block data is the concatenation of the slice payloads, and it includes the parent slot and the parent hash. The paper says there are limits on a block, including a bound on its bytes and a bound on its execution time. The block hash is the root of a second Merkle tree. That tree is the smallest complete full binary tree whose leaf count is a power of two and is at least the number of slices. The first leaves are the slice roots, each marked as a leaf, and the remaining leaves are empty. An ancestor is any block reached by parent links, including the block itself. If one block is an ancestor of another, the other is its descendant.

sections.heading: 2.2 Rotor
paragraphs: Rotor disseminates a block from the leader to the other nodes. The goals are low latency, balanced use of bandwidth, and resilience to transmission failures, with the block produced and sent as a stream so the leader need not wait for the whole block. Each slice is one independent round, sent when it is ready, which pipelines production and transmission. For a slice the leader produces Γ Reed-Solomon shreds, hashes them into a Merkle tree, and signs that tree's root. Each shred includes its Merkle path and the root signature, with as much data and metadata as fit in one UDP datagram. Any γ shreds reconstruct the slice. The receiver then generates the missing shreds as an additional validity check.

Relays are sampled for every slice by a method the paper says improves resilience and specifies later. The leader sends each shred directly to its relay. The relay then sends that shred onward to the remaining nodes, largest stake first, skipping itself and the current leader. A small speedup delivers the shred to the following leader before the others, since that leader is the party that needs the data soonest. Authenticity is checked per shred. The leader's Merkle tree and root signature make that check local. On the opening shred of a slice, a node verifies the path and the signature and stores the root. On later shreds it checks only the path against the stored root.

A latency figure reports average and median Rotor latency for γ equal to 32 and for total shred counts 64, 80, 96, and 320, using the sampling defined later. Reference lines mark average or median network latency. At expansion 10, hence 320 shreds, the paper says the result is close to the single-delay latency of the latency lemma. Every curve in that figure uses Solana stake from epoch 780. Latencies come from public measurements. The plotted times leave out both computation and the time spent transmitting bytes.

Rotor is successful for a slot when the leader is correct and at least γ of the relays are correct. Then every correct node receives the block. A faulty leader can send nothing, and Rotor fails immediately, so the resilience discussion assumes a correct leader. The paper says Rotor is likely to succeed if coding shreds are over-provisioned by at least "67%", written as κ equal to Γ over γ and strictly greater than "5/3". The resilience lemma says that if γ tends to infinity, a slice is received correctly with probability 1. Relays are chosen at random according to stake. Under the crash assumption each relay fails with probability under 40%", so the expected number of correct relays is at least "60%" of Γ, which is strictly more than γ. A Chernoff bound is applied for the infinite-γ step.

The latency lemma says that if Rotor succeeds, network latency is at most "2δ", and that a high expansion can reduce it. With the node count and the expansion both tending to infinity, the paper says latency can be brought down to δ. The sketch is that relays receive their shred from a correct leader within δ and correct relays forward it within another δ. With enough over-provisioning, and under what the paper calls natural assumptions on stake distribution, at least γ correct relays lie between the leader and the receiver. If they sit on the direct path they add no overhead, and the two legs sum to δ. The same latency figure is cited as simulation on Solana's stake distribution.

The bandwidth lemma assumes a fixed leader sending at a rate no higher than average outgoing bandwidth, and any distribution of outgoing bandwidth proportional to stake. It claims that every correct node then receives block data at the leader's rate divided by κ, in expectation, and that this is optimal up to κ. A node is a shred relay, in expectation, in proportion to its stake. The leader splits its bandwidth across the relays, so the node receives from the leader in proportion to its stake and must forward that data to the other n minus 2 nodes. Its outgoing bandwidth, proportional to stake and scaled by n times the average, is enough for that forward rate when the leader does not exceed the average.

The same proof says the delivered rate cannot rise above the leader's rate, because only the leader knows the data at the start, and cannot rise above average outgoing bandwidth, because every node must receive the data and total sending capacity is n times that average. Apart from the expansion, the paper calls the construction optimal. It also says attacks on Rotor may affect liveness only. The other parts of Alpenglow are what provide safety under asynchrony, and they rely on Rotor only to disseminate data.

sections.heading: 2.3 Blokstor
paragraphs: Blokstor keeps whichever block Rotor delivers first for each slot. A shred is added when that slot, slice, and shred index is not already present, the data and path match the slice root, and the signature is the leader's signature on the slice identity. When the first complete block for a slot arrives, Blokstor emits a block event with the slot, the block hash, and the parent hash, as input to the voting loop. It can also repair and store some other block. If a block is finalized for a slot, only that block is collected and stored for the slot. Before the safe-to-notarize event for a block, that block has to be in Blokstor as well.

sections.heading: 2.4 Votes and Certificates
paragraphs: The voting summary uses two thresholds. If at least "80%" of stake votes for the leader's block, the block is finalized immediately after one round by a fast-finalization certificate. A node that sees notarization stake reach "60%" casts the follow-up vote. Once that second vote itself totals "60%", the block is final as well. Stake that collectively treats the block as overdue can assemble a skip certificate and drop the proposal.

Five vote objects are each signed by the voting node. A notarization vote and a notar-fallback vote name the slot and the block hash. A skip vote and a skip-fallback vote name the slot. A finalization vote names the slot. Certificates aggregate stake. Fast-finalization requires notarization votes of at least "80%". Notarization requires notarization votes of at least "60%". Notar-fallback counts notarization or notar-fallback votes of at least "60%". A skip certificate counts skip or skip-fallback votes of at least "60%". Finalization requires finalization votes of at least "60%".

sections.heading: 2.5 Pool
paragraphs: Each node keeps a Pool of the votes and certificates it has for every slot. It stores, per slot and per voting node, the first notarization or skip vote, up to three notar-fallback votes, the first skip-fallback vote, and the first finalization vote. When enough votes have arrived for a certificate type, the Pool generates that certificate. A certificate that is newly received or newly constructed is broadcast to all other nodes. One certificate of each type is stored for the given block or slot. The paper notes that generating a fast-finalization certificate implies the notarization certificate, which implies the notar-fallback certificate.

Finality can arrive on either of two certificates. When the Pool holds a finalization certificate for a slot, the single notarized block of that slot becomes final; the document names that outcome slow-finalized. When it instead holds a fast-finalization certificate on a block, that block becomes final under the name fast-finalized. Ancestors finalize before the block itself. The Pool also emits a block-not-notarized signal when enough evidence shows that no notarization will form. If the present slot is the opening slot of a leader’s window, a timeout certificate may appear after the timeout rules fire. Those certificate names and window rules are the protocol’s definitions in this file.

The safe-to-notarize event for a block means it is no longer possible that a different block is fast-finalized in the slot, so a notar-fallback vote is safe. It is issued only if the node has already voted in the slot and did not vote to notarize this block. The stake condition is that notarization stake on the block is at least "40%", or that skip stake plus that notarization stake is at least "60%" and notarization stake is at least "20%". On the first slot of the window the event is emitted when the condition holds. On a later slot the block is retrieved by repair first, so the parent can be identified, and the event is emitted when the Pool also contains the parent's notar-fallback certificate. Stake of any node is counted only once per slot.

The safe-to-skip event means it is no longer possible that any block in the slot is fast-finalized, so a skip-fallback vote is safe. It is issued only if the node has already voted and did not vote to skip. The test adds skip stake to notarization stake over all blocks in the slot and subtracts the largest single-block notarization stake. The event requires that remainder to be at least "40%".

sections.heading: 2.6 Votor
paragraphs: Voting notarizes and finalizes blocks. Finalized blocks are a single chain of parent references and are the output of the protocol. For every slot, the paper says either a skip certificate appears, or else some block is notarized or notarized-fallback, with all ancestors of that block notarized as well. Thresholds are there so a malicious leader cannot prevent the certificates liveness needs. If many correct nodes produce notarization votes for the same block, all other correct nodes make notar-fallback votes for it. Otherwise all correct nodes broadcast skip-fallback votes. A node can finalize once it has seen a sufficient notarization tally. The paper states the participation again: one round across an 80%-stake cohort, or else two rounds among nodes with "60%".

participants keep local clocks and raise timeout events. The first parent-ready event for a window starts timeout timers for every slot of that window. Two delays are used. One is the protocol block time. The other is the rest of the possible delay, besides the block time, between arming timeouts and obtaining a correctly disseminated block. As a conservative global constant, the paper says that second delay can be set to one ∆ plus two ∆, above the time for the leader to observe the certificates plus Rotor latency.

The timeout for a slot in the window is the local clock plus that delay plus the block time multiplied by the slot's position in the window, counting the first slot as one. Because parent-ready is emitted only for the first slot, the multiplier is at least 1 and the timeout is never scheduled in the past. The deadlines correspond to the latest arrival when the leader behaves and synchrony holds. They can be optimized, including for crash faults.

Votor keeps per-slot state, initially empty, and a list of pending blocks, initially empty. State can permanently record parent-ready for a hash, that a notarization or skip vote was cast, that this node notarized a particular hash, that a notarization certificate is held, that the finalization vote was cast, or that the window is bad. The finished mark means no further votes will be cast in the slot. The bad-window mark is set when the node has cast a skip vote, a skip-fallback vote, or a notar-fallback vote. Pending blocks are blocks to be revisited, because the notarization condition may become true later.

The event loop is single-threaded. On a block event the node tries to notarize and on success, checks pending blocks. If it has not voted, it stores the block as pending. On a timeout, if it has not voted, it tries to skip the window. On a notarized-block event it records the certificate and tries to finalize. On parent-ready it records the parent, checks pending blocks, and starts the timers for the window. On safe-to-notarize it tries to skip the window and if it has not finished the slot, broadcasts a notar-fallback vote and marks the window bad. On safe-to-skip it tries to skip the window and if it has not finished, broadcasts a skip-fallback vote and marks the window bad.

A notarization vote is possible only if the node has not yet voted. On the first slot of a window, parent-ready must be recorded for the parent hash. On a later slot, the node must have notarized the parent in the previous slot. It then broadcasts the notarization vote, records the voted marks, clears the pending block, and tries a finalization vote as well. The finalization vote is broadcast only when the notarization certificate for that hash is recorded, the node itself notarized that hash, and the bad-window mark is absent. Casting it records that the slot is finished. The skip helper walks every slot of the window and where this node has not voted, broadcasts a skip vote, marks the slot voted and bad, and clears the pending block so it will not notarize after skipping. Pending blocks are retried in increasing slot order.

sections.heading: 2.7 Block Creation
paragraphs: The leader of a window produces blocks for every slot in the window. After parent-ready for a parent hash, the leader can be sure a block in the first slot with that parent will be valid, because other nodes will receive the same certificates and emit the same event, so all correct nodes will vote for the block. In the common case one such event is emitted and the leader has to build on that parent. If many parent-ready events are emitted for different blocks, because the previous leader misbehaved or the network delayed messages, the leader may build on any of them.

An optimization lets the leader start before any parent-ready event. Usually the previous block arrives first and the certificate arrives after a further network delay. If the leader started on one parent and then only sees parent-ready for a different block, it indicates the new parent in the content of some slice. Earlier slices of that block are ignored for execution. The indicated parent may be changed only once, and only in the first slot of a window.

Once the leader has observed some parent-ready event, it produces the rest of the window without delays. The first block builds on a parent for which parent-ready was emitted, and each later block in the window parents the next. The procedure waits until the block in the previous slot is received or parent-ready is in state, then generates slices while parent-ready is still absent. If the ready parent is not the optimistic parent, it selects any ready parent, regenerates the block from the current slice index, and continues. It then produces the rest of the block for one block time. Each remaining slot is a new block parented on the previous block, disseminated by Rotor over one block time.

The handover figure shows the new leader starting the first slice of its first block once it already holds the last slice of the previous leader, and a second case in which the parent changes and the block starts from a different parent at a later slice. In a practical implementation, some payload space is reserved for certificates that prove an earlier block reached finality. Into that space the leader puts proof of the newest block it has seen become final: the fast certificate by itself, or the slow finalization certificate plus the notarization certificate. Those certificates are a permanent record for observers who do not participate in the protocol directly.

sections.heading: 2.8 Repair
paragraphs: Repair retrieves a block of a stated hash absent from Blokstor. It is required after the Pool obtains a certificate on a notarization or a notar-fallback for that hash, because the block with that hash then has to be retrieved. A contact is chosen at random based on stake. One call returns the number of slices and the hash at the last slice position, with its path under the block hash. The requester checks that this hash is the last non-empty leaf and that rightward hashes in the path correspond to empty subtrees. Another call returns the hash and path of a chosen slice. A third returns one shred for a slot, slice, shred index, and slice root. Any call can fail verification, including when the contact returns invalid data or does not have the data, and then the result is empty.

The repair procedure asks random stake-weighted nodes for the slice count until the answer verifies. For every slice, concurrently, it fetches the slice hash until that hash verifies. For every shred index, concurrently, it fetches the shred until a valid shred is stored. The stored shred is the one returned for those indices and for the slice root already accepted.

sections.heading: 2.9 Joining
paragraphs: Open membership has to let machines enter and exit. The paper treats a restart, a crash, and any other interruption as the same re-entry problem, because over a long run every machine will stop at least once. A joining or returning node has missed the messages sent while it was offline. If it observes finalization of a block in a slot, it does not need votes or certificates from earlier slots, because ancestors are finalized implicitly.

Safety implies that any later finalized block is a descendant of the block just observed, so a later parent-ready parent has to be a descendant as well. The rejoining node needs either a fast-finalization certificate or a (slow) finalization certificate together with a notarization certificate, for a block in some slot. Repair retrieves that block. After it is stored, the parent can be identified and retrieved, and so forth. A practical build ought to fetch missing blocks for all slots in parallel.

sections.heading: 3 Correctness
paragraphs: The correctness section proves safety and then liveness, and then discusses a high number of crash failures. Safety is the claim that correct nodes do not finalize conflicting blocks when delays are arbitrary. Liveness is the claim that correct nodes finalize new blocks from correct leaders once the network is synchronous and dissemination succeeds. The crash discussion relaxes the fault assumption and adds a condition on what two correct nodes can reconstruct. A later subsection of the same section proves a bound on how many blocks a correct node stores per slot.

sections.heading: 3.1 Safety
paragraphs: A certificate exists, in this analysis, when a correct node has observed it. An ancestor of a block exists in a slot when collision resistance of the hash implies that following parent links from the later block reaches that ancestor. If a certificate exists, correct nodes holding at least a reduced stake threshold have cast the corresponding votes. Byzantine nodes hold less than "20%", so the correct stake is more than the certificate threshold decreased by "20%". The derived table says fast-finalization requires correct notarization votes above "60%". Notarization, notar-fallback, skip, and finalization each require correct stake above "40%" on the vote types that certificate accepts.

A correct node casts only one notarization vote or one skip vote per slot. Both are cast only while the voted mark is absent, and casting either sets the mark. If a block is fast-finalized, no other block in the slot can be notarized, no other block can be notarized-fallback, and no skip certificate can exist for the slot. Correct nodes holding more than "60%" cast notarization votes for the fast-finalized block, so they cannot notarize a different block or skip. Notarization stake on any other block is therefore smaller than "40%". A notar-fallback vote is cast only on the safe-to-notarize event, which needs at least "40%" notarizing the rival or at least "60%" notarizing the rival or skipping, and only the complement, under "40%", can cast those votes. A skip-fallback needs at least "40%" skipping or notarizing a different block, which that complement cannot supply, and the fast-finalizing nodes do not skip.

If a correct node cast a finalization vote in a slot, it issued neither a notar-fallback nor a skip-fallback ballot there. The finalization vote sets a finished mark that later fallbacks require to be absent, and a fallback sets a bad-window mark that the finalization vote requires to be absent, so neither order is possible. If correct nodes with more than "40%" notarize one block, no other block in the slot can be notarized, because a notarization certificate needs "60%" and would require some node in that set to have notarized both blocks. At most one block is therefore notarized in a slot. If a correct node finalizes a block, a notarization certificate of that block exists. On the fast path, correct nodes with more than "60%" broadcast notarization votes. On the slow path, finalization votes are cast only after a notarization certificate has been observed, and uniqueness says that certificate is for this block.

Slow-finalization has the same three exclusions. Correct nodes holding more than "40%" cast the finalization votes, each of them already saw a notarization certificate covering that same block, and each had cast a notarization vote for it and no other vote in the slot. Because those nodes hold more than "40%" and every certificate needs at least "60%", no skip certificate and no certificate on another block in the slot can be produced. Separately, either a notarization certificate or a notar-fallback certificate covering a block implies that some correct node cast a notarization vote for it. Otherwise every correct node would observe less than "20%" notarizing it. Both parts of the safe-to-notarize condition require observing "20%" notarizing the block, so no correct notar-fallback vote would be cast, and a certificate needs "60%".

If a correct node notarizes a block, then in every earlier slot of the same leader window it notarized the ancestor in that slot. The first slot of the window has no earlier slot inside the window. A later notarization is cast only when the node has recorded a notarization of the parent hash in the previous slot, and that record is written only when the notarization vote is cast. If a block is notarized or notarized-fallback, every earlier slot of its window contains an ancestor for which either correct nodes with more than "40%" cast notarization votes, or else an honest node issued a notar-fallback ballot. The first case follows from the window-ancestor property. The second starts from a correct notar-fallback vote, which the safe-to-notarize rule issues only after a notarization or notar-fallback certificate on the parent, and the claim continues by induction.

Suppose a correct node finalizes a block, and another block in the same leader window, in the same or a later slot, has a notarization or notar-fallback certificate observed by any correct node. The paper concludes the later block is a descendant. The slots differ, by the finalization properties. Some correct node notarized the later block, hence notarized an ancestor in every earlier slot of the window. The ancestor in the slot just after the finalized block has a different parent in the finalized slot. A notar-fallback vote on that ancestor would mean the different parent is notarized or notarized-fallback, contradicting the finalization properties. Notarization votes from correct stake above "40%" on that ancestor would mean those nodes also notarized the different parent, contradicting uniqueness.

The cross-window claim uses the same hypotheses with the certified block in a different, later window. Take the highest ancestor of that block which is still at or after the finalized slot and which is notarized or notarized-fallback. If it shares the finalized block's window, the previous lemma applies. Otherwise some correct node notarized an ancestor in the first slot of that later window, which required parent-ready on its parent, so the parent is notarized or notarized-fallback. If that parent is before the finalized slot, the Pool holds a skip certificate for the finalized slot. If it is in the finalized slot, the finalization properties fail again. A later parent would contradict the choice of the highest ancestor.

The safety theorem follows from those lemmas. If any correct node finalizes a block in slot s, and whenever an honest node finalizes a block in a slot at least s, the later block is a descendant of the earlier one, because the later block is notarized and both the same-window and cross-window arguments apply.

sections.heading: 3.2 Liveness
paragraphs: If a correct node emits parent-ready for the first slot of a window, it emits a timeout for every slot of that window, because the handler schedules those timeouts. A timeout for a slot therefore implies parent-ready on the first slot of its window. Whenever every honest node arms the timeout on a slot, all of them cast a notarization vote or a skip vote there. The timeout handler calls the window-skip function unless the node has already voted, and the voted mark is added only by a notarization or a skip. If no honest cohort whose stake exceeds 40%" notarized the same block, no correct node marks the slot finished. That mark is added only after a notarization certificate, which needs that correct stake.

If all correct nodes set the timeout, then either all of them eventually observe a skip certificate, or correct nodes with more than "40%" cast notarization votes for the same block. If no such notarizing set exists, every correct node observes skip or notarization votes from correct stake of at least "80%". After those votes arrive, skip stake plus all notarization stake equals "80%" plus any stake outside that correct set which was also observed, and the largest notarization stake is at most "40%" plus that outside stake. The safe-to-skip difference is therefore at least "40%". A node in the correct set that has not skipped emits safe-to-skip. It has no finished mark, so it casts a skip-fallback vote. All correct nodes thus cast a skip or a skip-fallback, and all observe a skip certificate.

If correct nodes with more than "40%" notarize a block, all correct nodes observe a notar-fallback certificate for it. The argument inducts on the distance from the first slot of the window. A correct node that will not notarize or notar-fallback the block still sees the "40%" and emits safe-to-notarize. It cannot have a finished mark, because that mark follows a finalization vote for a notarized block, and no other block in the slot can be notarized. It therefore casts the notar-fallback vote. On a later slot the same node retrieves the block, identifies the parent, and the induction hypothesis gives a notar-fallback certificate on the parent before safe-to-notarize is emitted. Hence, whenever every honest node arms timeouts on a window, every slot of the window yields a notar-fallback certificate or a skip certificate, observed by all correct nodes.

Those timeouts also imply that all correct nodes emit parent-ready for the first slot of the next window. If every slot of the current window is skipped, the notarization or notar-fallback certificate that justified the current window, plus skip certificates through the new window start, meets the parent-ready rule. If some highest slot is not skipped, its notar-fallback certificate plus the skip certificates after it meets the same rule. By induction from these two facts, all correct nodes set the timeouts for all slots. After the network has stabilized, if the first correct node set the window-start timeout at time t, all correct nodes emit some parent-ready for that window and set the timeouts by t plus ∆. That first node had already observed the certificates, broadcast them, and delivery after stabilization is within ∆.

The liveness theorem takes a correct leader of a window that starts at slot s. No correct node set the window's timeouts before stabilization, and Rotor is successful for every slot of the window. The claim is that blocks produced by that leader in every slot of the window are finalized by all correct nodes. The first step times delivery. Let t be when the earliest honest node arms the timeout on s. Then t is at least the stabilization time, and by one ∆ the leader has parent-ready and has reached the timed production loop. It finishes transmitting the block of slot k by t plus ∆ plus the block time times the slot's index in the window. Successful Rotor delivers that block by t plus three ∆ plus the same block-time term.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that some correct node does not notarize the leader's block in a lowest slot k of the window. The leader is correct, so that block is the only valid block any party receives in the slot, and the node casts a skip. It also skips every later slot of the window, because a notarization there requires a recorded notarization of the parent. Skip votes come from the window-skip helper, after safe-to-notarize, safe-to-skip, or a timeout.

Whichever of those three caused this node's first skip in the window, it is the timeout on k. Safe-to-notarize cannot fire for a correct node on a slot before k, because every correct node notarized the leader's block there, and on slot k or later the event requires a skip already cast. Safe-to-skip is excluded by the same reasoning. A timeout on an earlier slot would not skip anything, because the node had already notarized there, and later slots time out later. The earliest first skip is therefore the timeout on slot k.

That timeout is emitted no earlier than t plus the timeout parameter plus the block time times k's index in the window. With the conservative parameter, this is at least t plus three ∆ plus the block-time term, which is the delivery time already calculated. By then the node has received every leader block from the window start through k, has parent-ready recorded for the window parent, and the notarization condition holds. Pending blocks are retried when a block event or a parent-ready event is handled, so the node has notarized every block through k regardless of arrival order. That contradicts the choice of a node that skipped k. Therefore every correct node notarizes every block of the window, observes the fast-finalization certificate, and finalizes the block.

sections.heading: 3.3 Higher Crash Resilience
paragraphs: This section sketches correctness when the network is less adversarial and more nodes have crashed. In harsh network conditions the paper says an adversary with over "20%" of stake can attack Alpenglow, and that such an attack requires careful orchestration. It says accidental errors, crashes, and DoS campaigns, treated as functionally akin to crashes, have historically hurt blockchain deployments more often. The rest of the section uses Assumption 2 in place of Assumption 1, plus Assumption 3. That assumption says that when an honest node obtains a complete block through Rotor, every other honest node that obtains a complete block through Rotor during that slot obtains that identical block. Crashed nodes are treated as equivalent to indefinite delay. Safety was shown for arbitrarily large delays, so the paper says safety holds under Assumption 2.

Liveness reasoning changes where it depends on correct nodes observing enough votes to trigger safe-to-notarize or safe-to-skip. With the added assumption that two correct nodes cannot reconstruct different blocks in the same slot, the paper says that once every correct node has seen the other correct votes, each of them fires one of the two safe events. When correct notarization stake on one block is at least "20%", the combined test holds: skips plus that notarization reach "60%", and the notarization itself is at least "20%". Otherwise the safe-to-skip expression is at least the skip stake, and the skip stake is at least "40%". A corollary says the liveness theorem holds under Assumptions 2 and 3. A correct leader, and a crashed leader, each emit at most one block in a slot, so the non-equivocation assumption holds for them. The paper therefore treats pure crashes below "40%" of stake as always inside the liveness claim.

The section then sketches when Assumption 3 can fail: an adversary distributes different blocks to different parties. If many nodes have also crashed, honest nodes may lack sufficient votes to raise either safe event, . The protocol could stall. Imagine a malicious leader distributes two blocks so so one honest cohort rebuilds and backs one while others reconstruct and vote for the other. If a correct node receives two shreds that do not belong to the same block, with different Merkle roots for the same slice index, before it can reconstruct, it will not vote. Network topology and the sampling of Rotor relays determine whether two different blocks can be delivered to different correct nodes.

The example uses two clusters of correct nodes. Latency inside a cluster is negligible relative to latency between the clusters. Each cluster holds "31%" of stake. The adversary controls "18%", and "20%" is crashed. Relays in the first cluster receive shreds of one block, relays in the second receive shreds of another, and adversarial relays forward each block only inside its cluster. Each cluster reconstructs its block before observing any shred of the other, so Assumption 3 fails. The paper says a more even geographic spread makes it harder for a big group to collect a full reconstructing set of one version while still missing every shred of the rival version.

sections.heading: 3.4 Bounded State
paragraphs: This subsection limits how many distinct blocks can reach notarized-fallback status inside one slot, and how many a correct node must retain. When a correct node issues three different notar-fallback votes aimed at three different blocks, every notar-fallback ballot from an honest node targets one of those three. The document says the only first-round layout that forces an honest node to cast three distinct notar-fallback votes also forces every other honest node into the same trio. From that bound the text argues that each correct node stores only a constant number of candidate blocks per slot. The bound is a proof claim in the paper; it was not re-checked here as a live cluster property.

The proof normalizes stake to 1 and writes byzantine stake as f, strictly below 0.2 by Assumption 1. Honest skip stake, and honest notarization and notar-fallback stake on each block, are separate quantities. Correct nodes' first-round votes are disjoint, so honest skip stake plus honest notarization stake over all blocks is at most 1 minus f. On one block, notarization and notar-fallback from the same node are disjoint, so the stake that voted either way is their sum. A certificate needs at least "60%" of notarization or notar-fallback stake at some observer, which is more than 0.4 after subtracting f. The safe-to-notarize condition, rewritten with byzantine stake, requires honest notarization stake at least 0.4 minus f, or at least a quantity the paper shows is still strictly above zero. A notarized-fallback block then needs both the certificate-sized sum and honest notarization stake strictly above zero.

Another lemma starts from four or more blocks that correct nodes have notarized. Each correct node then fallback-votes at most two of them. If a correct node does cast them for two distinct blocks, honest skip stake plus honest notarization stake on those two is at least 0.8 minus f. The two-block cap is called a corollary of the three-block lemma. The numeric inequality considers how byzantine stake must be split across the first-round views the node saw. In each of the view combinations the paper lists, disjointness of skip stake and the two notarization stakes yields the same lower bound.

The bounded-notarize-fallback lemma says that for any slot, at most four distinct blocks are ever notarized-fallback. Assume five, and combine the stake-sum bound with the certificate inequality on each of them. Because each correct node contributes at most two fallback votes, the resulting inequality forces honest skip stake to be at most twice f. Consider the graph whose vertices are the five blocks and whose edges are pairs that some correct node fallback-voted. The graph has an edge: with no edge, each node would contribute at most one fallback vote, and skip stake would come out negative, which is impossible. Two disjoint edges are also impossible. They would force skip stake to be at least 0.8 minus 2f, and together with the cap of 2f that forces f at least 0.2, contradicting Assumption 1.

A family of pairs in which every two pairs intersect is a star or a triangle, and the proof uses a vertex cover of that graph. Every edge meets the cover, so each correct node contributes at most one fallback vote to the blocks outside the cover. For a star, one block joined to four others, the resulting honest-stake sum is negative. For a triangle, with the cover an edge and three blocks outside, the sum contradicts the two-block inequality, because 0.8 minus f is greater than 0.2 plus f when f is below 0.2. Five notarized-fallback blocks are therefore impossible. This is the paper's proof that vote thresholds limit how many conflicting blocks one slot can certify.

An execution shows the bound of four is tight. Stake is counted out of 45. Three groups of 6 notarize the first, second, and third blocks respectively, and each fallback-votes the other two of those three. Three groups of 1 notarize a fourth block and fallback-vote three different pairs among the first three. A group of 17 skips and fallback-votes the fourth block. A group of 7 equivocates. The paper states that 7 of 45 is under "20%". Everyone sees 18 of 45, equal to "40%", in skip votes. The groups that fallback-vote two of the first three blocks each see 9 of 45, equal to "20%", notarizing each of those two, using the remaining byzantine stake split into two groups of 3. The skipping group sees 9 of 45 notarizing the fourth block. No correct node casts conflicting votes.

In that execution the first three blocks each have 6 notarization votes and 21 notar-fallback votes, totaling 27. The fourth has 3 notarization votes and 24 notar-fallback votes, also 27. Because 27 of 45 equals "60%", each block gets a notar-fallback certificate. The storage corollary caps a correct node at seven different blocks in one slot. A block is kept if Rotor delivered it, if repair followed a safe-to-notarize pattern, or if repair followed a notarization or notar-fallback certificate. Rotor contributes at most one. The paper says the safe-to-notarize case is largest when skip stake is "40%" and three separate blocks each have "20%" notarization stake, which is three blocks. At most four notar-fallback certificates can be created. The sum of one, three, and four is eight.

The paper then rules eight out. If a node stores three blocks from the safe-to-notarize case, the three-block lemma says all nodes see a subset of those same three blocks in the certificate case. The total in that situation falls, and storing eight blocks is impossible. The tighter bound stated is that a correct node stores at most seven blocks per slot.

sections.heading: 4 Severe Failures
paragraphs: Safety and liveness are guaranteed under the fault assumptions and under bounds such as message delay. If more nodes deviate, the system may behave incorrectly, and the paper says the deviation can occur without adversarial intent. One source is implementation diversity. Several independently developed clients may intend to implement the same specification. If nodes split between two clients that are about equally adopted, and the clients execute a transaction differently, they disagree on the system state. From either client's perspective, roughly half the nodes appear to behave arbitrarily, exceeding the fault tolerance threshold. Safety or liveness may then fail even though no node is intentionally faulty.

The paper states the diversity tradeoff directly. Greater client diversity raises divergence risk, and a more uniform client set raises the chance that one bug hits many machines together. A systemic failure is many machines failing at roughly the same time because they experience the same problem. Individual node failures are handled by the joining procedure. Systemic failures are a more serious challenge, and the next subsections discuss network failures and software failures.

sections.heading: 4.1 Systemic Network Failures
paragraphs: The model assumed delayed messages are eventually delivered and that delay is eventually at most ∆. The paper says real networks, and the original formulation of partial synchrony, can lose messages, and that serious interruptions such as regional power outages can break the delay bound. Two mechanisms are discussed for large packet loss or persistently increased delay. Safety with dropped messages is already claimed, because the protocol handles arbitrarily large delays. The mechanisms address liveness.

Eventual delivery is what liveness after stabilization needs. As in the joining discussion, a correct node that has observed a finalization in a slot needs no vote or certificate messages for earlier slots in order to proceed. Missing liveness is detectable by a period with no new slots finalized. After a parametrized time with the highest finalized slot unchanged, the example is "10 sec", correct nodes retransmit. What they resend for the newest finalized slot is either the fast-finalization certificate alone, or the slow finalization certificate paired with the notarization certificate. For every higher slot they broadcast observed certificates and their own votes. They also emit parent-ready for the latest finalized block that sits in the first slot of a leader window. That emission is there so nodes are not stuck missing certificates before the retransmitted finalization, which the routine omits.

A standstill might last a full epoch. The protocol is defined for one epoch in the partial-synchrony model, and message delays may be arbitrarily long, but epochs themselves are finite. Moving to the next epoch, the paper says requires that epoch to contain at least one finalized block. That block closes the prior epoch on one agreed state and fixes who the validators are and what they stake, when the epoch after next begins. The response to persistently large delay is to extend timeouts.

Still seeing no fresh finalized block after that same "10 sec", a node begins stretching every leader window's timeouts by "5%". Nodes need no coordination to extend. As soon as they see finalized blocks again, they can return immediately to the standard timeouts, and the paper says some nodes may still use longer timeouts without jeopardizing correctness. The "5%" increase compounds. The paper says the resulting growth becomes longer than any extraordinary delay from a network or power disaster, so a slot is finalized in each epoch.

Even with that growth, nodes may accumulate hundreds of votes and non-finalizing certificates since the last finalization if the standstill is long. Flooding hundreds of all-to-all messages repeatedly is described as an order of magnitude above regular Votor communication, and the network is likely already unstable. Each node therefore limits its sending rate. It cycles through the messages and certificates since the last finalized slot, and it sends that slot's finalization information repeatedly during the cycle, with once per twenty cycling messages as the example. As soon as it finalizes a higher slot, it jumps to that slot and cycles from there.

sections.heading: 4.2 Systemic Software Failures
paragraphs: Correlated software failures are listed as client bugs from edge-case transactions, plus specification ambiguities, in which two clients behave differently on the same input, and buggy updates that break one client. The paper says these failures are serious, since they more readily yield Byzantine failures, which adhere to the lower tolerance of "20%". It asks whether every client implementation can be kept under "20%" of stake. In a permissionless system operators choose the client, so the paper says a "20%" limit is difficult to enforce. Different clients may also share libraries or operating-system routines. It calls a guarantee that every bug affects less than "20%" of stake practically inconceivable, and it points to recent outages of large operators as the pattern it has in mind for the bulk of recent system outages.

To detect a split in execution state, some state commitment has to enter protocol messages. Votes on blocks could include a commitment to the state from executing the block, or blocks could include the commitment the leader computed. If a bug causes divergence, nodes count other nodes voting on differing commitments. After a delay with no progress, a minority can emit a special abstain, naming the slot where the states diverged. Any certificate may count these abstentions, and its threshold shrinks in proportion to the stake that abstained. Liveness can be restored by the minority dropping out. Safety then pertains only to the nodes that did not abstain. The example says that abstentions of "45%" would leave safety covering "20%" of the other "55%" of stake, which the paper calculates as "11%" byzantine stake.

sections.heading: 5 Quantumglow: Post-Quantum Security
paragraphs: The paper flags elliptic-curve primitives used by Alpenglow, including EdDSA and BLS, and says elliptic-curve designs fail against an adversary capable of quantum computation. Naively substituting post-quantum signatures is rejected because the design assumed the small signatures of EdDSA and BLS. The adaptation is called Quantumglow. It eliminates aggregate signatures and uses only single-signer digital signatures that are meant to be post-quantum. Certificate-pool synchronization then uses additional approval messages, so certification is less self-contained. The paper claims that common-case performance is preserved: fast-finalization latency and communication complexity remain unchanged.

sections.heading: 5.1 Choice of Primitives
paragraphs: The survey says many primitives remain effective against practical quantum computers, in particular symmetric encryption, message authentication, and cryptographic hash functions. The paper says these are believed to remain secure, and it stresses that cryptography rests on computational-hardness assumptions. Grover's algorithm can give a quadratic speedup for brute-force search and does not, on this account, break the primitives. The loss is compensated by larger keys and digests. Hash-based constructions and proofs are said to have been studied in the quantum setting. Elliptic-curve signatures do not carry over. The design still wants core protocol messages to fit in one MTU-sized packet. If QUIC is used in datagram mode, "1,160" bytes remain for payload, compared with "1,200" bytes for plain UDP.

A table lists candidates by signature size, public-key size, NIST security category, signing-side risk, and verification speed. Falcon-512 has a "666 B" signature and an "897 B" public key, category 1, high signing risk, and fast verification. The paper calls it the smallest standardized post-quantum signature shown. XMSS-SHA2 20 192 has a "1.7 KB" signature and a "52 B" key, category 3, moderate risk, and fast verification. ML-DSA-44 has a "2.4 KB" signature and a "1.3 KB" key, category 2, low risk, and fast verification. SLH-DSA-128 has a "7.9 KB" signature and a "32 B" key, category 1, low risk, and slow verification. The signing risk column covers secret-state reuse for XMSS and side-channel leakage for Falcon and SQISign.

Non-standardized schemes in the same table include SQISign, with a "148 B" signature and a "65 B" key, category 1, high risk, and slow verification, and Hawk-512, with a "555 B" signature and a "1.0 KB" key, category 1, low risk, and fast verification. A cited break, which the paper says the scheme's authors accepted, leads it to treat the Hawk-512 parameters as insecure. Other standardized signatures in the table do not fit the packet. Hawk is described as closely related to Falcon and as eliminating floating-point sampling in signing, which can leak the secret key without constant-time guarantees.

Quantumglow sends large signatures with small accompanying data, for example an index, a hash, plus a message type, about "40 B". Any scheme with a signature below "1,120 B" can be used, including Falcon-512 along with assorted XMSS parameter sets. The named XMSS-SHA2 20 192 signatures are too large, while XMSS-like hash-based constructions can be parametrized. The next subsection designs a custom scheme. The paper says signatures still impose overhead that demands a protocol redesign, and that feasible solutions exist.

BLS is called a more serious problem. A vote carries one BLS signature. A certificate compresses a whole quorum into one aggregate, and both still fit beside their payload in a single packet, with a bitmap naming the signers on the certificate. No constant-size aggregate signature with post-quantum security is known, on the paper's account. Dedicated constructions that exist scale logarithmically with signer count, yet with large constants, only slightly more efficient than concatenation at about "1,500" nodes. Attempts based on zero-knowledge proofs of all individual verifications are described as the same order of magnitude in size, with prover latency on the order of seconds.

A comparison at about "1,000" signers includes BLS. Naive Falcon-512 is "666 B" per signature and at most "666 KB" concatenated, with aggregation essentially free and verification at most "40 ms", growing linearly in the number of signers. Lemur is about "78 KB" for one signature and about "185 KB" aggregated, about one second to aggregate and about "15 ms" to verify. leanMultisig is about "1.5 KB" and about "400 KB", about two to three seconds to aggregate and about "30 ms" to verify. Falcon-512 with LaZer is "666 B" and about "70 KB", about "500 ms" to aggregate and about "250 ms" to verify. BLS is "48–192 B" both for one signature and for the aggregate, about "1 ms" to aggregate and about "0.3-0.5 ms" to verify. The paper calls the aggregate-signature situation bleak and removes the need for aggregation in the Quantumglow voting design.

sections.heading: 5.2 Ax: Integrated Hash-based Signatures
paragraphs: Hash-based signatures are argued to fit this setting if they are integrated with the protocol, which is how the paper proposes to handle signature size and key management. What it wants back is post-quantum strength at the high end that still fits inside one packet of MTU size. The instantiation is called Ax, short for Alpenglow XMSS. A one-time signature begins with a secret seed. Repeated hashing derives intermediate secret values and a public key. Signing reveals a subset of the intermediate values determined by the message hash. The verifier applies the one-way function and checks the public key. Each signature discloses part of the secret material, so the key pair is used once. Reuse on a second message reveals further values and lets an attacker combine them to forge signatures on other messages.

The paper considers Winternitz one-time signatures, specifically W-OTS+, and compares constant-sum encodings with target-sum grinding. For a verification-bounded workload it prefers the ability to trade verification cost for signing cost, and it does not treat deterministic signing as the main advantage. Security is fixed at "192 bits", described as the first level viewed as stronger than 256-bit hash collision resistance already used in the protocol. That level uses 24-byte public keys at NIST's category 3. A table of target-sum parameters, measured for an optimized implementation on an Apple M4 Max, varies the Winternitz width and the target sum. Signatures are "1,168 B" at width 16, "952 B" at width 32, "784 B" at width 64, "688 B" at width 128, and "592 B" at width 256, with "24 B" public keys throughout.

Each width is shown with a lower target sum and a raised one. At width 32, target 604 signs in "11.5 µs" and verifies in "9.4 µs", while target 781 signs in "202 µs" and verifies in "7.5 µs". Higher targets spend signing time to reduce verification time, and higher widths shrink the signature while raising both times. The recommendation is width 32, which the paper says minimizes verification cost while still fitting the hard per-packet ceiling of 1,120 B", together with a raised target such as 781, about 2 to the 14 grinding steps on average, to trade still more verification cost versus signing cost. With these parameters, verifying "1,000" signatures takes about 7.5 ms on one core.

Some messages need no full signature. Skip, skip-fallback, and final votes, and skip and final approvals carry solely the vote type plus the slot number as payload, and the public key is already tied to those fields. They are described as signing a zero-bit message. Opening one committed secret is enough to authenticate them, which makes each of these signatures "24 bytes". The per-slot table allows one each of the final, skip, and skip-fallback votes at that size, one notarization vote and up to three notar-fallback votes at full signature size, one skip approval at "24 B", and one notarization approval plus up to four notar-fallback approvals at full size. The notar-fallback cap cites the four-block lemma.

The key figure is for one validator and one epoch of length "18,000". Each slot reserves nine one-time keys and four zero-bit commitments, matching the per-slot table. Public values sit in binary Merkle trees of ceiling of log base 2 of 13 levels, which the paper computes as 4, under a tree of ceiling of log base 2 of 18,000 levels, computed as 15, for 19 levels in total. One root public key per validator and epoch is committed on chain. Before the epoch, each validator reliably sends all of these public keys to all other validators. The paper writes the volume as 13 times 18,000 times 24 bytes and states it as "5.36 MB". Other validators check the received keys against the on-chain root.

The usual downside of stateful hash-based signatures is key management: a one-time key must not sign more than one message. Here that duty is mapped to equivocation, so a node that does not equivocate also never reuses an one-time key. In the usual XMSS mode the public key is a Merkle commitment and each signature includes both the one-time signature and the Merkle path. Signing k messages under capacity K reveals k times log base 2 of K hashes for the paths, while using the one-time keys directly reveals K hash outputs once. For dense signing, with k near K, the paper says the path mode is inefficient in total bandwidth, so Ax uses the one-time keys individually and omits the paths, at a total cost of k plus K.

Where it matters for external verifiers, the Merkle root is still defined as the public key and the paths are added to the signature. Only that root is registered on chain. Validators are assumed to exchange and cache one another's one-time public keys ahead of time, and therefore to hold the public part of each Ax tree. Not sending the public keys is treated as equivalent to invalidating one's own signatures. Not storing them is treated as equivalent to a byzantine node dropping signatures it received. The paper says these changes are neutral to correctness.

sections.heading: 5.3 Rotor
paragraphs: Original Rotor has the leader sign every slice root and place that signature, plus a Merkle path, inside every shred, so one shred can be checked on its own. EdDSA is short enough for the shred to stay inside one MTU packet. A post-quantum signature alone would occupy over half that packet. Adding the path would push cryptography past two-thirds of the shred. The paper says the higher bandwidth is theoretically feasible and practically inefficient, and a figure contrasts an Alpenglow shred, a naive quantum-resistant shred carrying a Falcon-512 signature, and a Quantumglow shred. Quantumglow reduces the overhead by relaxing independent verifiability of shreds.

Each shred still includes its Merkle path and no longer includes a signature. Dropping the signature cuts per-shred cryptographic overhead from "256 B" down to "192 B". On arrival, a validator recomputes the root from the path that came with the shred. Once shreds for a given slice have arrived root, they reconstruct the slice. In place of shred signatures, the leader sends a block commitment once each block finishes, to authenticate the block. The commitment includes the same fields a notarization vote carries, and may count as a notarization vote when tallying, so it is exactly a notarization vote. It is sent through Rotor relays for fault tolerance and equivocation detection, without erasure coding. The leader sends a copy to all relays, and the relays forward it to all nodes. The dissemination figure shows coded slices and then copied commitments.

The commitment maintains the difficulty of equivocating and of distributing different blocks to different correct parties, which the paper says matters when failure rates top 20% of stake.
