If the leader tries to equivocate, it must sign two incompatible commitments, called a slashable offense. They also stop a big colluding relay set from inventing a block and attributing it to the leader.

Nodes rely on symmetric authentication to store only shreds forwarded by valid relays. Without leader signatures in the shreds, they cannot be sure the shreds come from the leader. Bad data slices are disclosed once the slot ends, when the commitment arrives. If the block hash in the commitment does not match the slices, nodes vote to skip. All nodes can still optimistically execute slices as they are received. Byzantine relays may produce fraudulent shreds that do not match the leader. This can be discovered when a slice is received, because the root derived from a malicious path fails to match that shred, or yields another slice root when assembling a slice, a node considers only shreds that match the predominant slice root.

A Quantumglow shred has the same fields as an Alpenglow shred except the root signature, in the order slot, slice index, shred index, root, data and path, and flag. A slice has slot, index, root, decoded payload, and flag, again without the signature. A block is defined as in Alpenglow and is made of these slices, and the block hash is defined exactly as before. For a block of k slices, the commitment binds the leader, in an attributable way, to that block and to every one of the k slice bodies. To simplify the design, the message is a notarization vote on the slot and the hash, signed by the leader of the slot.

After broadcasting all k slices, the leader sends Γ copies of the signed commitment to Γ relays, drawn by the same random rule used to pick slice relays. Those relays pass the commitment along exactly as they pass shreds. A validator emits the block event only after also receiving at least γ matching commitments from different relays. If it receives two valid but conflicting commitments, it has evidence of leader equivocation, invokes the window-skip procedure, and slashing is possible. As soon as it sees γ copies, it may also begin block repair when needed. If a correct node casts a notarization vote for a block, it holds a valid block commitment for that block, because a correct validator casts the vote only after emitting the block event, and it emits that event only after receiving and verifying γ commitments.

If a block gets a notar-fallback certificate, the corollary says it was produced by the leader of the slot. If two different blocks get notar-fallback certificates in the same slot, two correct nodes hold valid commitments that together prove leader misbehavior. If fewer than γ relays are byzantine, every correct node eventually sees valid commitments for both blocks. Only byzantine relays send to some validators and not to others, so successful equivocation requires at least one correct relay for each commitment, and those correct relays eventually deliver both messages to all validators.

The last lemma of the subsection says that a successful equivocation leaves two distinct correct validators holding two disjoint message sets from one Rotor instance, each set received before any message from the other set. The paper says that challenge matches the hardness of equivocating under Alpenglow. There, it is enough to make two correct nodes reconstruct different versions of the last slice, and commitments are checked in essentially the same way as signed shreds.

sections.heading: 5.4 Votor
paragraphs: Alpenglow's voting relies on aggregate BLS signatures over votes and certificates. Because no practical quantum-proof aggregate is available, Quantumglow uses a different communication pattern. The solution is presented inside Alpenglow and is described as more general, applicable to other consensus protocols and more broadly in distributed systems. It is not tied to the "20+20" model. A companion paper is cited for the general discussion. Quantumglow uses no aggregate signature scheme. Certificates become two notions, a weak cert and a strong cert. Weak certs are Pool-recorded events. They signal safety for the linked blocks or skips. They are not broadcast and are not network messages, so they might appear at some nodes yet not propagate to other correct nodes. A strong cert is also a safety record, with the extra claim that every correct node eventually stores it. The pool records both and interfaces the changes to the rest of the protocol.

Approval messages synchronize the strong-cert pool. A validator sends an approval to all other validators when it has recorded a weak cert. An approval indicates a certificate type and is signed by a single node. The paper's example is a notar-fallback approval of a slot and a block hash. Fast-finalization and finalization certificates are not associated with an approval. The approvals that are defined pair a notarization certificate with a notarization approval, a notar-fallback certificate with a notar-fallback approval, and a skip certificate with a skip approval. The pool records approvals received from other nodes.

A weak cert is recorded the first time one of two conditions holds. Votes matching the original certificate threshold are observed, or approvals for it have arrived from at least "20%" of stake. When a weak cert is recorded, the node broadcasts the corresponding approval. A strong cert is inserted once matching approvals cover at least "60%" of stake. The figure of this rule shows the vote threshold or the "20%" approval path inserting the weak cert and broadcasting the approval, and the "60%" approval path inserting the strong cert. A notarization certificate already constitutes a notar-fallback certificate. To save bandwidth, a notar-fallback approval need not be broadcast with every notarization approval, and a notarization approval counts as both when certs are recorded.

Protocol interactions of the old certificate pool are swapped for interactions against the weak-cert pool, except that the weak-cert pool never emits parent-ready. The strong-cert pool emits parent-ready, analogously to the certificate pool in Alpenglow. The timeout delay is increased to account for slower strong-cert synchronization through approvals. The paper says increasing that delay by one ∆ is enough. As a conservative constant it can be set to two ∆ plus two ∆, above the time for the leader to observe certificates plus Rotor latency.

sections.heading: 5.5 Quantumglow Safety
paragraphs: The next two subsections analyze Quantumglow. As in the original correctness section, they argue safety and liveness under Assumption 1, and the paper says the crash-section remarks apply unchanged. Saying a certificate exists still means some correct node observed it. Saying a block is notarized or notarized-fallback means at least one honest node saw the matching certificate. The correct-voter lemma is restated for weak and strong certs: if one exists, some set of correct nodes holds at least the reduced stake from the earlier table and has cast the corresponding votes.

Suppose a correct node observed a weak cert, and let one correct node be the first in the execution to observe it. Either that node saw votes matching the original creation threshold, and the result follows as in the original lemma by subtracting byzantine stake of less than "20%" from those thresholds, or it observed the weak cert after approvals from nodes with "20%" of stake. The second case contradicts the choice of the first node. Byzantine stake is less than "20%", so some correct node broadcast the approval earlier, and an approval is broadcast only upon observing the weak cert. when an honest node has seen a strong cert, the definitions imply it also observed the corresponding weak cert.

The safety theorem is stated again. If any correct node finalizes a block in slot s, and whenever an honest node finalizes a block in a slot at least s, the later block is a descendant. The original lemmas from the single notarization-or-skip vote through the same-window descendant lemma, and the original safety theorem, follow when certificates mean weak certs and the new voter lemma is used as the old one was. Parent-ready is governed by strong certs, so the cross-window lemma follows with that reading: certificates relevant to parent-ready are strong certs, and holding a strong cert already implies the weak cert was seen. Every other certificate mention in that argument stays on the weak side.

An attribution lemma says that when any honest node creates a weak cert, some possibly different correct node holds cryptographic evidence that sufficient stake voted to form it. By the previous proof, some correct node first created the weak cert by observing votes that match the original threshold. Each of those votes is individually verifiable proof that the signer cast it.

sections.heading: 5.6 Quantumglow Liveness
paragraphs: The timeout lemma, the single notarization-or-skip lemma, the lemmas that force a skip certificate or a notar-fallback certificate, and the corollary that a timeout implies parent-ready on the window start, all follow after two adaptations. The new voter lemma is invoked in place of the old one, and the certificates considered are weak certs. Those proofs omit certificate broadcast, which Quantumglow no longer has. when every honest node sees a weak cert, all of them broadcast the corresponding approval. Because they hold more than "60%" of stake, all of them observe the strong cert.

If a correct node emits parent-ready at a time t after stabilization, all correct nodes emit the same parent-ready by t plus two ∆. The node that emitted it had, for every strong cert the event depends on approvals totaling at least "60%" of stake. Under either fault assumption, correct stake of at least "20%" had already sent each of those approvals by time t. One ∆ later, all correct nodes have received those approvals, and they broadcast their own approvals. By t plus two ∆, all correct nodes have received approvals from all correct nodes, observed the strong certs, and emitted the same parent-ready event.

whenever every honest node arms timeouts on a window, all of them emit parent-ready for the next window. The original argument for that step counts only certificates every honest node has observed and does not rely on certificate broadcast. The corresponding weak certs are observed by all correct nodes, so the strong certs are observed as well, and parent-ready is emitted. By induction, all correct nodes set the timeouts for all slots.

After stabilization, if the earliest honest node armed the timeout on the first slot of a window at time t, all correct nodes emit the same parent-ready and set the window timeouts by t plus two ∆, because that first node had emitted parent-ready and the two-delay lemma spreads it. The liveness theorem matches the original wording: a correct leader, no pre-stabilization timeout for the window, and successful Rotor on every slot, imply that all correct nodes finalize the leader's blocks. The proof follows the original proof, using the Quantumglow timeout lemmas, the larger timeout constant, and the one-∆ difference in the parent-ready bound. Because the timeout constant is also larger, the paper says the statement of the theorem is unaffected.

A transferability lemma says that when any honest node creates a weak or strong cert, it can produce a message of size linear in the number of nodes that is cryptographic proof that creating the cert is safe. The node bundles the votes or approvals that caused the cert. There is at most one per node, each of constant size, so the total is linear, together with an indication such as a bitmap of which items were included. For each contained vote or approval, a non-conflicting item is counted as though the signer had sent it directly, and an item from a signer already proved malicious is subtracted from the stake the receiver still requires.

sections.heading: 5.7 Securing the Rest of the Stack
paragraphs: Apart from core consensus, non-quantum-secure cryptography is used for authenticated channels and for transaction signatures. For channels, the paper says adequate post-quantum key-exchange standards already exist, for example the standardized ML-KEM-768, whose ciphertext fits in a single MTU-sized packet. Requirements are not very strict, because under normal operation channels between nodes are reused for at least an entire epoch. Symmetric encryption is treated as post-quantum secure, except that AES-128 is weaker than the level wanted here, which is why AES-192 is the smallest symmetric cipher the paper names.

Transaction signatures have less stringent requirements, so the paper allows standardized designs including ML-DSA-44 and Falcon-512. Asking users to track one-time hash keys is treated as impractical. A standardized signature is preferred because wallets and hardware devices must implement it, not only the validator code. Accounts are currently indexed by Ed25519 public keys of "32 B". For a post-quantum scheme with a different public-key size, the key can be mapped into the same space by a 256-bit hash, with SHA-256 as the example. A cited construction migrates from an EdDSA key pair to a post-quantum key pair even after EdDSA has been broken, using the seed from which the secret key is derived as a witness inside a proof of knowledge. On that account, accounts can wait to move until after EdDSA fails. Cheaper alternatives exist when a one-time migration that reveals the seed is acceptable.

Certificates in Alpenglow also prove finalization to third parties outside consensus. That can be done by sharing the necessary "80%" notarization votes, or the "60%" notarization votes and "60%" finalization votes, or more compactly, the 20% notarization approvals together with the 60% finalization votes. One-time public keys are shared among nodes to make vote signatures smaller, and only the root public key is registered on chain, so a proof shown to an outsider must attach, with every signature, that one-time key and the sibling hashes linking it to the on-chain root. The standstill procedure has to be adapted because certificates are no longer network messages. Each validator rebroadcasts recent votes and approvals of its own when progress stalls for long enough. Nodes then synchronize by building certificates locally out of votes or approvals, under the Quantumglow rules.

sections.heading: 6 Beyond Consensus
paragraphs: The closing section describes issues that are not the core of the consensus protocol and still deserve attention. It starts with relay sampling and with execution, both close to consensus, and finishes with parameter choices and with simulation results for bandwidth and latency. The paper presents the section as background for understanding Alpenglow, separate from the safety and liveness proofs.

sections.heading: 6.1 Smart Sampling
paragraphs: To improve Rotor's resilience in practice, the paper uses a committee sampling scheme inspired by a published construction and intended to improve on that construction's independent fallback by reducing variance further. A partitioning of relative stakes into k bins is a map that assigns each node a share of each bin. For every node, the shares over bins sum to that node's stake. For every bin, the shares over nodes sum to 1 over k. A partitioning algorithm computes a valid partitioning for any number of bins and any positive relative stakes. Partition sampling, called PS-P, is instantiated with one such algorithm and generates Γ samples in three steps.

Any node whose relative stake exceeds 1 over Γ fills a number of bins equal to the integer part of its stake times Γ. Its remaining stake is then strictly below 1 over Γ. The symbolic expression for that remainder is flattened in the extract. The prose states the filled count and that the remainder is below 1 over Γ. Every smaller node keeps its original stake as the remainder. The chosen algorithm partitions those remaining stakes into the bins that were not filled. From each bin, one node is sampled proportional to its stake in the bin. One simple partitioning algorithm randomly orders the nodes and cuts exactly after every 1 over k of relative stake. Even this simple cut, the paper says already improves on the cited committee scheme, and it calls for more work on the sampler.

Let the adversary control total stake possibly spread over many nodes, and assume that total is below γ over Γ, which the paper sets equal to 1 over κ. For any stake distribution in which every individual stake is below 1 over Γ, and for any partitioning algorithm, the chance the adversary is drawn at least that many times under PS-P is no more the chance in independent stake-weighted sampling. For any partitioning, the number of adversary samples is Poisson binomial: the number of successes in Γ independent trials that may have different probabilities. The success probability of a trial is the adversary's share of that bin. If the adversary is packed equally in all bins, the count is binomial with success probability equal to the adversary's stake, the same distribution as independent stake-weighted sampling. The paper says that binomial case maximizes the variance of a Poisson binomial and therefore maximizes the probability of at least γ samples.

For an arbitrary stake distribution, the chance the adversary is drawn at least that many times under PS-P is no more the chance in the cited scheme's independent fallback. The first step, filling whole bins for large stakes, makes the scheme equivalent to that earlier scheme with partition sampling as its fallback, so the previous lemma applies.

The practical comparison uses the current Solana stake distribution. The figure shows the probability that Rotor is not successful under crash failures, for PS-P with fully randomized partitioning, compared with the earlier fallback, stake-weighted sampling, and Turbine. It assumes 64 slices per block, so the block succeeds only if every slice succeeds. One panel uses 32 data shreds and 64 total shreds and marks crashed stake at "40%", "30%", and "20%". The other fixes "40%" crashes and expansion 2, and marks total shred counts of 64, 128, and 256. Failure probability is on a logarithmic scale. The extract does not print a numeric height for each curve.

sections.heading: 6.2 Voting vs. Execution
paragraphs: The protocol section omitted execution of blocks and of the transactions in them. The paper says Solana currently uses the synchronous execution model it then describes. Under the eager model the leader runs the block first and only then ships it, and every other node runs it before casting a vote. That adds execution latency on the critical path. Slice dissemination is pipelined, so the next slice propagates while the previous slice executes. In the common case, only execution of the last slice adds latency before a node may issue a notarization ballot. In lazy, or asynchronous, execution, many protocols ballot on blocks without executing them, and execute the finalized blocks afterward. Some checks are still performed before voting. A compute-unit metric has to reflect actual execution cost and indicate that the block will be executed in time. When those units mis-estimate cost badly, execution latency may grow without bound.

Many consensus protocols that adopt lazy execution assume a block's validity can be checked from metadata about its ancestors, such as certificates, without observing the parent block. Consensus can continue finalizing while nodes retrieve missing blocks in the background. The paper calls this convenient in theory and lists practical downsides. A leader that has neither seen nor run its ancestors can repeat data, miss invalid transactions, and miss unpaid fees. Running transactions before the vote avoids those gaps and yields state sooner, which the paper ties to uses such as trading. The cost is speculative state: several candidate states may be kept, and the ones that lose are thrown away, which makes the implementation harder.

Eager mode also forces a node to fetch and run ancestor blocks before it may build or vote. That can affect consensus. If a leader must produce a block and has not reconstructed or executed the parent, repair or execution latency might prevent a timely block and cause a skipped slot. Should Alpenglow be paired with eager execution, the paper suggests two adjustments to dissemination. Whenever an honest node rebuilds a block it could forward a shred at random, based on stake, to the next few leaders. If many voters reconstruct the block, the probability that some later leader needs to repair it would be negligible. Separately, the number of shreds required for reconstruction could be lower than the number that results in voting. If many nodes vote, any node that has not voted can then reconstruct with high probability without repairing.

sections.heading: 6.3 Protocol Parameters
paragraphs: Parameters introduced through the paper are collected for the preliminary simulations, and the paper says testing is needed to decide them ultimately. Some are implicit and differ every epoch, in particular the number of nodes. The paper used about "1,500" nodes through the text and says the live count, when the paper was written, was nearer about "750". The simulation table sets 4 blocks per leader window, 32 data shreds per slice, 64 coding shreds per slice, a timeout increase of "5%", a maximum of "2,000" nodes, a standstill trigger of "10 sec", a block time of "200 ms", and an epoch length of "18,000" slots.

sections.heading: 6.4 Bandwidth
paragraphs: Bandwidth analysis starts from estimated sizes of voting messages for a network of "1,500" nodes. Column headers in the size table are misaligned in the extract. The component widths and the row totals are readable. A BLS signature contributes 96 bytes, a slot number 8, a block hash 32 when present, a node bitmap 188 on certificates, a message authentication code 16, and headers 28. The totals are 180 bytes for a notarization vote, 368 for a notarization certificate, 368 for a fast-finalization certificate, 148 for a finalization vote, 336 for a finalization certificate, 148 for a skip vote, and 336 for a skip certificate.

As an optimization, only one finalization certificate is broadcast, whichever is observed first. Ordinarily, each slot causes every node to send one notarization vote, one finalization vote, one notarization certificate, and one of the two finalization certificates. Accounting for the larger finalization certificate, the fast-finalization certificate, the paper computes 180 plus 368 plus 368 plus 148 bytes, times "1,500", for every "200 ms" slot, and states "63.8 Mbit/s". A histogram shows up-bandwidth for a consistent goodput of "500 Mbps", where leading requires transmitting at 1 Gb/s for expansion 2. Validators are ordered from small stake to large, and Rotor and Votor are separate series, on a logarithmic megabit scale. Individual bar values are not tabulated.

Quantumglow message sizes are estimated the same way. A notarization or notar-fallback message is "1,036" bytes, from a "952" byte signature, an 8 byte slot, a 32 byte block hash, a 16 byte authentication code, and 28 bytes of headers. A final or skip message, including the fallback forms, is "76" bytes, from a "24" byte signature and the same framing without a block hash. An approval is the same length as the vote of the matching kind. For "1,500" nodes the paper computes two times "1,036" plus one times "76", times "1,500" bytes, every "200 ms", and states "129 Mbit/s". The sentence giving the common-case broadcast also names a notarization vote and approval, a fast-finalization approval, and a finalization vote and approval.

A comparison table gives maximum message size and communication cost per node per slot, for the good case, with Quantumglow using the width-32 one-time signature. At "1,000" nodes, aggregate BLS is "261 B" and "762 KB", Falcon-512 plus LaZer is about "70 KB" and about "70 MB", and Quantumglow is "1,036 B" and "2,176 KB". At "10,000" nodes the same columns are "1,386 B" and "30.1 MB", about "70 KB" and about "700 MB", and "1,036 B" and "21.8 MB". At that larger count the paper judges Quantumglow roughly as cheap, in communication, as Alpenglow with pre-quantum aggregates. A figure plots maximum message size and communication per node per slot against the number of nodes, for Alpenglow and for Quantumglow at width 32 and at width 256. Width 32 is identified with faster verification and width 256 with smaller messages. Coordinates of the curves, beyond the table, are not listed.

sections.heading: 6.5 Latency
paragraphs: The latency runs use the Solana stake of epoch 780, the distribution current when the paper was written, and inter-node delays taken from measured networks. Outbound capacity follows stake. The largest stake is assigned "100 Gbit/s", the extract's verb there is misspelled, and no node is given less than "1 Gbit/s" outbound. Some delays are omitted, in particular block execution time. A different stake distribution would change the results. For a leader located in Zurich, each bar is the average over "100,000" simulated executions, and Rotor relays are drawn at random by stake weight. The plot is latency against the fraction of stake that has reached each stage.

Network latency is one stage. With the current Solana node distribution, about "65%" of stake is within "50 ms" round-trip of Zurich, and the long tail has more than "200 ms" of network latency from Zurich. That latency is a lower bound for the plot: a node whose path from Zurich is already "100 ms" cannot see finality any sooner than that under this protocol or any other. The next stage is Rotor, the time at which nodes have gathered enough shreds to rebuild a slice, the next stage is the time a node has received notarization ballots covering at least 60% of stake. Finalization is the last stage. A node finalizes by constructing a fast-finalization certificate from "80%" of the original notarization ballots, or else a finalization certificate from "60%" of the finalization votes, or by receiving one of those certificates from a third party, whichever is first.

For the fixed leader in Zurich the paper states that the last node finalizes in less than "200 ms", and that the median finality, roughly "110 ms", sits close to the fastest nodes in the histogram. A second histogram uses the same network parameters and samples the leader randomly by stake in each iteration. Zurich is described as more central than the average leader, so the numbers are higher, and median time-to-finality sits near 130 ms". A third plot compares Quantumglow finalization times with Alpenglow finalization times for random leaders. The caption states the comparison and does not give a separate numeric gap.

Apart from network transmission, the other main latency overhead the paper discusses is cryptographic calculation, most notably signature verification. A final figure compares the computation Alpenglow and Quantumglow do per slot, counting signatures over the block's slices and signatures in the votes. One panel fixes 100 slices and varies the number of nodes. The other fixes "1,000" nodes and varies the number of slices; both figures are extrapolated from micro-benchmarks on an Apple M4 Max, with logarithmic axes. Width 32 is again the faster-verification setting and width 256 the smaller-message setting. The paper does not tabulate the curve values. It ends the section by thanking a list of people for their input. That acknowledgment states no protocol result.
